title: Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015
short_title: Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015

speeches.speaker: Bruce Billson
speeches.brief: The Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015 was moved to establish a statutory ombudsman to advocate for and assist small businesses and family enterprises, citing over 2 million small businesses (96% of all businesses) producing $330 billion and employing 4.5 million people, while criticising the former Labor government for losing 519,000 small business jobs and reducing the small business workforce share from 52% to 43%.

speeches.speaker: Bernie Ripoll
speeches.brief: Labor supported the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015 but raised concerns that sections 67(2)(b), 67(2)(c) and 69(1) could limit the Ombudsman’s independence and impartiality, particularly in disputes between small businesses and government agencies. The speaker also noted that the bill’s provisions on termination of appointment lacked a statutory immunity clause and that the Ombudsman’s powers to hold hearings required ministerial referral.

speeches.speaker: Bert Van Manen
speeches.brief: The Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015 was announced with $8 million in funding over four years to create an ombudsman advocating for small businesses and family enterprises, which represent 97% of all Australian businesses. The ombudsman will reduce regulatory burdens, with estimated net economic benefits of $18 million per year, and assist businesses in the Forde electorate among others.

speeches.speaker: Jane Prentice
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015, arguing it fulfils a coalition election commitment to establish an ombudsman providing advocacy and alternative dispute resolution for small businesses. He contrasted the coalition's record—including small business tax cuts, instant asset write-offs up to $20,000, and $2.45 billion in red tape savings—with Labor's policies, which he criticised as unfunded and inconsistent.

speeches.speaker: Nola Marino
speeches.brief: The member supported the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015, arguing the ombudsman would act as a strong advocate for small businesses and family enterprises by reducing red tape, conducting investigations, and coordinating with state and territory bodies. The speech cited that small businesses make up about 97 per cent of all Australian businesses, employ around 4.6 million people, and account for 46 per cent of private-sector workers, with 210,000 small businesses in Western Australia and 12,716 in the member's own electorate.

speeches.speaker: Nola Marino
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015 will establish an impartial ombudsman with separate advocacy and assistance functions, including a concierge role to refer disputes and recommend alternative dispute resolution. The speaker cited personal experience with the ACCC's disrespectful treatment of dairy farmers after deregulation, noting the bill fulfills a coalition election commitment and reflects the government's support for small business.

speeches.speaker: Gai Brodtmann
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the two bills establishing the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman, noting Labor's previous initiatives such as the Australian Small Business Commissioner (Mark Brennan) and the National Business Names Registry, while urging the new Ombudsman to address government procurement problems including lengthy contracts, high insurance costs, and tender processes that disadvantage small and micro businesses.

speeches.speaker: Karen Andrews
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015, arguing it fulfills a 2013 election commitment to streamline dispute resolution and cut red tape, citing $2.4 billion in savings. The Ombudsman will serve as an advocate and concierge for dispute resolution, avoiding duplication of existing services, and the speaker noted over 2 million small businesses in Australia, with 96% of all businesses being small.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015 would support small businesses through advocacy and dispute resolution, which Labor supports, but criticised the government for politically exploiting small business issues, citing a $3.8 billion cut to small business and accusing the government of blocking its own legislation for political gain.

speeches.speaker: Karen McNamara
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015, which establishes an ombudsman to advocate for and assist small businesses and family enterprises, providing a single entry point for federal programs and dispute resolution. The government has delivered $2.45 billion in deregulatory savings and a $5.5 billion Jobs and Small Business package, with Australia’s two million small businesses producing over $330 billion in economic output and employing 4.5 million people.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: The Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015 was presented as a measure to restore the small business sector after 519,000 job losses and a decline from employing 53% to 43% of the private sector workforce under the previous Labor government. The speaker argued that the Ombudsman would address breakdowns in the rule of law, such as unfair contract negotiations and price discrimination, and called for reinstating triple damages in competition law while criticising the Harper review’s effects test and inadequate price discrimination provisions.

speeches.speaker: Nickolas Varvaris
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015 will create an ombudsman with advocacy and assistance functions to help small and family businesses cut red tape, with a concierge service and alternative dispute resolution referral. The speaker cited that small businesses represent 97% of Australian businesses, employ 4.6 million people, and spend $28,000 and 500 hours annually on compliance, and highlighted local examples in Barton, Kogarah, and Earlwood.

speeches.speaker: Michelle Landry
speeches.brief: The speaker announced the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015 and its consequential provisions bill, which establish a new ombudsman to advocate for, assist, and mediate disputes for small businesses. The speech also highlighted the $5.5 billion Growing Jobs and Small Business package, including a $20,000 instant asset write-off and a company tax rate cut to 28.5 per cent for businesses with turnover under $2 million, with the ombudsman expected to deliver net savings of $18.395 million per year.

speeches.speaker: Don Randall
speeches.brief: The Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015 creates an ombudsman to provide advice and dispute resolution for small businesses, citing 519,000 jobs lost under the previous Labor government and 21,000 new regulations introduced during that period.

speeches.speaker: Bruce Billson
speeches.brief: The Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill 2015 establishes a statutory ombudsman appointed by the Governor-General, with advocacy and assistance functions including early dispute resolution and referral of matters to other agencies. The government confirmed the ombudsman will not make binding decisions, and the opposition indicated its support for the bills.

speeches.speaker: Bruce Billson
speeches.brief: The Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman Bill allows the minister to redact or decline to publish ombudsman reports and advice to prevent release of information not in the public interest and to protect confidentiality of information provided by small businesses and family enterprises. The government welcomed opposition support for the bill, which fulfills an election commitment.
